title: Stocks Rally as Bessent Hails Successful China Talks Ahead of Trump‑Xi Meeting
body:
Global equity markets rose on Monday as investors cheered reports that Treasury Secretary Steven Bessent’s recent talks with Chinese Vice‑Premier Liu He were “productive,” bolstering expectations that the upcoming summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping in Washington could yield substantive progress on trade and other contentious issues. U.S. stock‑index futures pointed higher, while major Asian indices, including the Hang Seng and Shanghai Composite, posted modest gains, reflecting a broad‑based optimism that diplomatic momentum may finally translate into concrete policy moves.

Bessent, who met with Liu in Washington on Sunday, told reporters that the two officials “exchanged candid views on a range of topics” and that “there is a shared desire to see a constructive outcome from the forthcoming summit.” While he stopped short of detailing specific concessions, the language suggested a departure from the more confrontational tone that has characterized the bilateral relationship since the imposition of tariffs in 2018. Market participants interpreted the remarks as a signal that both sides are willing to engage in substantive negotiations, rather than merely staging a symbolic encounter.

The upcoming Trump‑Xi summit, scheduled for later this week at the White House, is being billed as a pivotal moment for the world’s two largest economies. Trade has dominated the agenda, with the United States seeking relief from what it calls unfair Chinese practices, including forced technology transfers, intellectual‑property theft, and market access barriers. Beijing, meanwhile, is looking to ease tariff pressures that have already cost Chinese exporters billions of dollars in lost revenue. Analysts also expect discussions on broader strategic issues—such as the status of North Korea’s nuclear program, regional security in the South China Sea, and cooperation on emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and 5G—to feature prominently.

The market reaction underscores how closely investors have tied financial performance to geopolitical developments. In the United States, the S&P 500 futures were up roughly 0.5% early Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite saw a 0.7% rise, reflecting particular optimism in the technology sector, which stands to benefit from any easing of export restrictions. In Asia, the Hang Seng Index climbed 0.8%, buoyed by gains in Hong Kong‑listed Chinese firms that have been hit hard by trade tensions. The Shanghai Composite added about 0.6%, suggesting that mainland investors are also hopeful that the summit could restore some stability to the export‑driven economy.

Nevertheless, caution remains among many policymakers and economists. The United States and China have a history of negotiating dead‑ends, and the “constructive outcome” Bessent described may be limited to procedural agreements rather than substantive tariff reductions. Moreover, domestic political pressures on both sides could constrain the leaders’ flexibility. In Washington, Trump faces a Republican base that has demanded a hard line on China, while in Beijing, President Xi must balance the need for economic openness with the Party’s emphasis on sovereignty and strategic autonomy. As a result, any agreement reached may be provisional, requiring further rounds of negotiation before implementation.

Looking ahead, the true test will come after the summit concludes. If the two presidents can agree on a framework that addresses core trade grievances and sets up a mechanism for ongoing dialogue, markets could see a sustained rally, especially in sectors most affected by the tariffs. Conversely, a stalemate or a vague joint statement would likely trigger renewed volatility, as investors reassess the risk premium attached to U.S.–China relations. For now, the positive market response reflects a collective hope that diplomatic overtures will finally break the impasse that has loomed over global trade for years, and that the Washington meeting could mark the beginning of a more stable, cooperative economic relationship between the two powers.
